hero.subtitle: Generate block-by-block blueprints for circles, ovals, spheres, and domes — with live preview, build order animation, and PNG downloads for Java and Bedrock.

home.answerTitle: What is a Minecraft circle generator?
home.answer1: A Minecraft circle generator is a free online tool that turns any diameter into a block-by-block pixel blueprint you can copy directly into the game. Pick a size from 5 to 256 blocks, choose a shape, and the generator draws the exact grid - every row, every block - for circles, ovals, spheres, domes and arcs in both Java and Bedrock editions.
home.answer2: The circle generator uses the same discrete-circle math as the midpoint circle algorithm, which is why odd diameters produce a clean, symmetric ring every time. No downloads, no accounts, and the blueprint is always free.
home.sourcesIntro: The circle generator is based on standard discrete-circle rendering, documented by the following public references:
howTo: Choose a shape and a size - odd numbers give a true center block.
Copy the blueprint block by block, or use Builder mode to step through every placement.
Export a PNG, SVG or copy /setblock commands with your world coordinates.
For spheres, domes, toruses and ellipsoids, build one layer at a time from the bottom up.

perSize.faqA3: Yes - every blueprint works identically in Java Edition and Bedrock Edition.
perSize.setblockBody: Open the generator and hit Copy /setblock to get every block as a Minecraft command. Add your world coordinates and the whole {shape} lines up exactly where you want it to be.
perSize.thicknessTip: Need a thicker wall? Set the outline thickness to 3-6 in the generator - a {d}-block ring with a thicker outline is much sturdier for castle walls and bases.
perSize.innerTip: Need a hollow ring? Use the inner cutout to remove the middle of the circle - perfect for moats, arenas and round towers.
perSize.builderTip: Build it block by block: turn on Builder mode in the generator to mark each placement with a click, step with Next and Prev, or press Play to auto-advance.

circle: Mark the center block, then place the four axis blocks at north, east, south and west.
Add the four diagonal corner blocks so the ring has 8 anchor points.
Fill each quarter section row by row, following the blueprint grid.
Check symmetry: each quadrant should be a mirror of the other three.
For a filled circle, move inward ring by ring until the center is covered.
sphere: Lay the widest ring as the equator first - it sets the size and shape.
Build the bottom half layer by layer, shrinking each ring toward the bottom cap.
Place a temporary pillar through the center to keep every layer aligned.
Build the top half with growing rings until you pass the equator.
Finish with the top cap, then remove the temporary pillar.
dome: Start with the full base circle on the ground, just like a flat circle.
Stack each next layer with a smaller ring, keeping the same center.
Follow the blueprint layer grid for the exact ring size of every layer.
Use slabs or stairs to smooth the curve as it gets steeper.
Close the top with the smallest ring and fill the center block.
oval: Mark the center and place the two long-axis end blocks.
Place the two short-axis end blocks at right angles to the long axis.
Fill each quarter arc between the axes, following the blueprint.
Mirror-check all four quarters for symmetry.
Rotate the whole oval 90 degrees to see how it fits your build.
torus: Start with the inner ring - the hole of the donut.
Build the ring cross-section at all 8 compass points.
Connect the cross-sections with the tube curve from the blueprint.
Work in the same horizontal layer all the way around.
Check the thickness: every tube segment must be identical.
ellipsoid: Lay the widest ring on the long horizontal axis first.
Build the depth-axis ring at right angles through the center.
Stack layers toward the top and bottom, shrinking the ring each time.
Keep the three axes symmetric - width, height and depth.
Smooth the surface with slabs where the curve is steepest.

materials.title: Materials needed
materials.intro: To build this {shape} you will need:

note.circle: All blocks sit at the same height, so lay the outline ring first, then fill the inside.
note.sphere: A sphere uses the most blocks for its size - every layer above ground needs scaffolding or a temporary center pillar.
note.dome: Layers shrink as you go up, so the ground ring uses the most blocks. A center pillar keeps every layer aligned.
note.oval: The long and short axes decide the look - a bigger difference makes a flatter, more elongated oval.
note.torus: The inner ring uses fewer blocks than the outer tube, so plan the hole size first.
note.ellipsoid: All three axes are different - the widest ring is horizontal, while the height and depth axes shape the rest.

items.q: How do I build a circle in Minecraft?
items.a: Pick a diameter, copy the blueprint from the grid, then place the blocks one by one. Start at the center block and work outward for a perfect result every time.

items.q: What circle size should I use?
items.a: Small circles (5-15 blocks) suit fountains and windows, 21-49 is right for towers and rooms, and anything above 65 is for huge builds like stadiums and coliseums.

items.q: Do the blueprints work for Java and Bedrock?
items.a: Yes. The grid shows block positions, so it works identically in Java Edition and Bedrock Edition.

items.q: How do I build a sphere or dome?
items.a: Switch to the sphere or dome tab, then use the Layer slider to see each slice from bottom to top. Build one layer at a time and the shape assembles itself.
Yes - hit Copy /setblock to get every block as a /setblock command, with your world coordinates applied. Use Copy All layers for spheres, domes, toruses and ellipsoids.
Builder mode turns the blueprint into a step-by-step guide: click blocks to mark them placed, use Next and Prev to move through the build order, or press Play to auto-advance.
